description:
verify_ocsp_responder (pkix-chain/src/lib.rs:1262-1266) has an explicit input guard:

    if chain.is_empty() {
        return Err(Error::OcspDelegation {
            reason: Cow::Borrowed("OCSP responder chain must contain at least the responder cert"),
        });
    }

The other seven wrappers (verify_tls_server, verify_tls_client_dns, verify_tls_client_mailbox, verify_smime_signer, verify_smime_recipient, verify_code_signer, verify_time_stamper) do NOT have such a guard. They rely on pkix-path::validate_path returning Err(NoTrustedPath) for empty chains (pkix-path/src/lib.rs:1561). The eight wrappers therefore have THREE distinct contracts for the same input:

- verify_code_signer: empty chain → Error::Path(NoTrustedPath) (validate_path catches it; no post-validation chain[0] access).
- 6 other wrappers (verify_tls_server, etc.): empty chain → Error::Path(NoTrustedPath) TODAY, but post-validation `&chain[0]` access (lines 772, 858, 935, 1003, 1036, 1157-1158) would PANIC if upstream behaviour changes. See PKIX-sqek.21 for the cross-crate invariant gap.
- verify_ocsp_responder: empty chain → Error::OcspDelegation { reason: "..." }.

WHY IT MATTERS:

The slash-command checklist for defensive-code-forcing calls out:

> API shapes that force every caller to write the same boilerplate defensive check. If 100% of callers will `if x.is_some() {` before doing anything useful, the API should have done that itself.

The inverse is also true: API shapes that produce a DIFFERENT error variant for the same input failure across a family of related functions force every caller to write per-function defensive code. A caller using all eight wrappers via a generic dispatch layer (e.g. "validate this cert under whatever profile is configured") has to match on three different error patterns for "empty chain":

    match wrapper_fn(chain, ...) {
        Err(Error::Path(pkix_path::Error::NoTrustedPath)) => "empty chain or no anchor matched",  // 7 wrappers
        Err(Error::OcspDelegation { reason }) if reason.contains("must contain") => "empty chain",  // 1 wrapper
        ...
    }

Worse, the verify_ocsp_responder variant is *misleading*: Error::OcspDelegation semantically means "the responder cert was not delegated by the named issuer." An empty chain is not a delegation failure; it is an input-validation failure. The wrapper has overloaded a variant to carry a separate failure class.

OPTIONS:

(a) **Add a dedicated Error::EmptyChain variant** (or `Error::InvalidInput { reason: Cow<'static, str> }` to admit other input-validation failures: empty anchors, malformed identity, etc.). Have all eight wrappers check at entry and return this. Document it in each wrapper's Errors section. Uniform contract; clean variant; defensive code is single-arm.

(b) **Use an input type that cannot be empty.** Replace `chain: &[Certificate]` with `chain: &NonEmptySlice<Certificate>` (workspace newtype) or with a tuple `(leaf: &Certificate, intermediates: &[Certificate])`. The compiler enforces non-emptiness; the error doesn't exist. Heavy-weight: every callsite has to construct the input.

(c) **Document the panic / upstream-dependency contract.** Every wrapper says "panics if chain is empty" (a lie — it doesn't panic today) or "returns Error::Path(NoTrustedPath) on empty chain" (true today, depends on upstream). Closes the documentation gap PKIX-sqek.21 raises but doesn't remove the OcspDelegation inconsistency.

The verify_ocsp_responder special-case suggests the maintainer ALREADY saw that "empty chain produces an obscure upstream error" is a defensive footgun, and patched it for the one wrapper. Generalizing the patch to all eight is the natural completion.

Closely related: PKIX-sqek.21 (chain[0] indexing depends on undocumented upstream gate). The two findings resolve together: option (a) here makes (a) for PKIX-sqek.21 trivially correct (empty chain returns Error::EmptyChain before chain[0] is ever touched).

Filed as priority 2 because empty-chain is the *cleanest* example of input-validation inconsistency, but the broader pattern (every wrapper has different defensive surface for malformed inputs) is the real cost. A single Error::InvalidInput variant fixes the family.
title: Wrapper empty-chain handling is inconsistent: 7 wrappers rely on upstream gate, 1 uses misleading Error::OcspDelegation variant
